questions.stem: Which of the following best defines culture?
options: The shared values, beliefs, customs and behaviours of a group of people
The level of education in a country
The artistic output of a nation
The language spoken in a market
questions.why: Culture covers religion, family structure, attitudes to gender and authority, and attitudes to time.
whyNot: Education is one influence on culture, not its definition.
The arts are one expression of culture.
Language is one element among many.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines an unintended meaning?
options: A meaning a brand name or slogan carries in another language that the business did not intend
A deliberate double meaning used in advertising
A translation error in a product manual
A claim that breaches advertising regulation
questions.why: The professional response is transcreation, recreating the intended effect, checked by native speakers in the market.
whyNot: That is intentional wordplay.
A manual error is a quality problem, not necessarily a meaning problem.
That is a regulatory breach.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines ethnocentrism?
options: Judging another culture by the standards of one's own and assuming what works at home will work abroad
Marketing only to one ethnic group
Employing only local staff in a foreign market
Adapting a product for each country
questions.why: It is the underlying error behind most cultural marketing failures.
whyNot: That is targeted segmentation.
That is a staffing policy, and often good practice.
That is localisation, the opposite error.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cultural consideration named in the specification?
options: Language and unintended meanings
The level of corporation tax
The reliability of the power supply
The rate of inflation
questions.why: The four named considerations are cultural differences, tastes and preferences, language and unintended meanings, and inappropriate branding and promotion.
whyNot: That is a fiscal factor.
That is infrastructure.
That is a macroeconomic factor.

questions.stem: Which element of advertising travels worst between cultures?
options: Humour, because it depends on shared reference points
The product photograph
The brand logo
The price shown
questions.why: Imagery, gender portrayal and religious references are also culturally specific and frequently misjudged.
whyNot: Product images generally travel reasonably well.
Logos are usually retained globally.
Prices are simply localised.

questions.stem: Why can religion affect a product decision?
options: Dietary rules, prohibited ingredients and modesty in imagery all constrain the offer
Religion determines the exchange rate
Religion sets the level of tariffs
Religion determines infrastructure quality
questions.why: Fasting periods and festival timing also drive seasonal demand patterns.
whyNot: Exchange rates are set in currency markets.
Tariffs are set by government.
Infrastructure depends on investment.

questions.stem: Which is an example of confusing cultural difference with income difference?
options: Explaining small pack sizes as a cultural preference rather than a matter of affordability
Adapting a product for religious dietary rules
Changing advertising imagery for local modesty norms
Translating a slogan with a native speaker's help
questions.why: Pack size, price point and purchase frequency are usually about income and retail structure rather than culture.
whyNot: That is a genuine cultural adaptation.
That is a genuine cultural adaptation.
That is a language adaptation.

questions.stem: Why is comparative advertising a cultural and regulatory risk?
options: It is normal in some markets and unlawful or considered rude in others
It is banned worldwide
It cannot be translated
It always increases sales
questions.why: Advertising content regulation is far stricter in some markets, especially for food, medicines and products marketed to children.
whyNot: It is lawful in many markets.
Translation is not the difficulty.
Its effect varies and can be negative.

questions.stem: Why does text expansion in translation matter?
options: It breaks packaging layouts, and right-to-left scripts change design entirely
It increases the tariff payable
It changes the product's ingredients
It makes the product heavier
questions.why: Script and direction are practical design constraints that catch businesses by surprise.
whyNot: Tariffs do not depend on label text length.
Labelling does not change the formulation.
Weight is unaffected.

questions.stem: Why is there no longer any such thing as a purely local campaign?
options: A campaign made for one market is visible everywhere within hours
All advertising must now be approved internationally
Local media no longer exists
Campaigns are legally required to run in every market
questions.why: An advertisement that offends in one country becomes a global reputational problem, which is the most useful modern point in this topic.
whyNot: No such approval requirement exists.
Local media is still substantial.
No such legal requirement exists.

questions.stem: Why must local staff be given authority rather than just consulted?
options: A business cannot see its own assumptions, so buying the information and overruling it wastes it
Local staff are legally entitled to make marketing decisions
Head office cannot communicate with local offices
Local staff are always more experienced
questions.why: A firm that hires local people and overrules them has bought the information and thrown it away.
whyNot: No such legal entitlement exists.
Communication is not the obstacle.
Experience varies; local knowledge is the specific asset.

questions.stem: Why is generalising about a whole region a mistake in this topic?
options: Cultures vary within countries as well as between them
Regions are defined differently by different governments
Regional data is never published
Marketing is always national by law
questions.why: Primary research in the specific market is what the answer should recommend, not desk research about a region.
whyNot: Definitional issues are not the substantive problem.
Regional data is widely available.
Marketing is not legally restricted to national boundaries.

questions.stem: How important are cultural factors compared with the other factors in this unit?
options: Decisive for food and media products, far less so for industrial components
Always the single most important factor
Never important where the product is well made
Important only in developing economies
questions.why: Saying which type of product is in the source, and therefore how much weight to give culture, is the comparative judgement that earns marks.
whyNot: Their weight depends on the product.
Product quality does not overcome cultural mismatch.
Cultural difference exists everywhere.

questions.stem: Which of the following reduces the risk of a cultural marketing error?
options: Pre-testing campaigns with local consumers before launch
Relying on desk research from head office
Using machine translation for all materials
Launching quickly to gain first-mover advantage
questions.why: Local research, local staff and agencies, and monitoring social media are the other safeguards.
whyNot: Desk research from home is exactly the weakness.
Machine translation misses meaning and connotation.
Speed without testing increases the risk.

questions.stem: What is the commercial cost of a withdrawn campaign?
options: The wasted production spend plus reputational damage that lasts considerably longer
Only the cost of the media space already bought
Nothing, because the campaign was stopped
A fine payable to the WTO
questions.why: The pattern is consistent: approved at home by people who did not know what it would mean elsewhere, and visible worldwide before anyone in the target market had been asked.
whyNot: Production, agency fees and the reputational effect all count.
The damage is done once it has been seen.
The WTO does not fine businesses.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines localisation?
options: Adapting a product, brand or campaign to suit the language and culture of a specific market
Producing a product within the market where it is sold
Employing only local staff
Registering a trademark in a local market
questions.why: It is the practical activity that glocalisation describes as a strategy.
whyNot: That is local production.
That is a staffing policy.
That is a legal step.
